items.stimulus: An ornithologist sketches a hawk's straight glide path, line $t$, as it crosses two parallel power lines, $m$ and $n$. In the figure, line $t$ intersects line $m$ and then line $n$. Where $t$ meets $m$, the angle above $m$ and to the right of $t$ is labeled $116^\circ$. Where $t$ meets $n$, the angle above $n$ and to the right of $t$ is labeled $x^\circ$. Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
items.stem: In the figure, line $m$ is parallel to line $n$. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: Both angles sit above their parallel line and to the right of the transversal, so they are corresponding angles. Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel, so $x = 116$.

A.why: You subtracted 90 from 116, as if the angles were complementary. Nothing in the figure makes a right angle.

B.why: You treated the angles as supplementary and found $180 - 116$. Angles in matching positions are equal, not supplementary.

D.why: You used the 360-degree rule for angles around a point. These two angles are at different intersections, and the rule doesn't apply to them.

items.stimulus: Two straight drainage channels cross each other at a single point, forming four angles. One of the four angles measures $50^\circ$. The angle directly opposite it, across the crossing point, measures $x^\circ$.
items.stem: What is the value of $x$?

D.why: You subtracted $50$ from $360$, which is the total of the other three angles around the point. You need only the single angle opposite.

items.subtype_name: Parallel lines / intersecting lines: one angle relationship
items.stimulus: A sheet of laminated composite has two parallel fiber layers, which appear as straight parallel lines in a cross-section. A straight crack crosses both layers, forming eight angles at the two crossing points. One of these eight angles measures $64^\circ$. A technician picks four of the eight angles, including at least one acute angle, and adds their measures.
items.stem: What is the greatest possible value of this sum, in degrees?
items.explanation: A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes only two distinct angle measures. One of them is $64^\circ$ and the other is $180 - 64 = 116^\circ$. Four of the eight angles are $64^\circ$ and four are $116^\circ$. If the four chosen angles include $a$ acute ones, the sum is $64a + 116(4 - a) = 464 - 52a$. The sum gets larger as $a$ gets smaller, and the condition requires $a \ge 1$. So the greatest sum uses one $64^\circ$ angle and three $116^\circ$ angles: $64 + 3(116) = 412$.

items.stimulus: In a nutrition science study, a cafeteria tray has two parallel straight edges that are crossed by one straight divider. The divider is not perpendicular to the edges, and the two crossings form eight angles. One of the eight angles measures $x^\circ$.
items.stem: Which of the following could NOT be the sum of the measures, in degrees, of four of these eight angles?
items.explanation: When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, it makes only two different angle measures: $x^\circ$ and $(180 - x)^\circ$. Four of each kind appear. If you pick $b$ angles that measure $180 - x$ and $4 - b$ angles that measure $x$, the sum is $(4 - b)x + b(180 - x)$. For $b = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$, this gives $4x$, $180 + 2x$, $360$, $540 - 2x$, and $720 - 4x$. The expression $360 - 2x$ is not on that list, so it can't be the sum.

A.why: You took the other angle measure to be $90 - x$ (the complement) when it is really $180 - x$. With the complement, sums like $3x + (180 - x) = 180 + 2x$ seem impossible. In fact, three angles of $x^\circ$ plus one angle of $(180 - x)^\circ$ give exactly this sum.

B.why: You made a slip when you expanded $x + 3(180 - x)$, so $540 - 2x$ looked like it couldn't happen. One angle of $x^\circ$ plus three angles of $(180 - x)^\circ$ add up to exactly $540 - 2x$.

C.why: You assumed four angles can't add up to more than 360°, as if all four had to sit at the same crossing. The four angles that measure $(180 - x)^\circ$ are spread over both crossings, and together they add up to $720 - 4x$.

items.subtype_name: Parallel lines / intersecting lines: one angle relationship
items.stimulus: A folklorist's sketch of a woven border motif shows two parallel threads crossed by a third straight thread, which makes eight angles. Four of these eight angles have a sum of $440°$. Exactly three of those four angles are congruent to each other.
items.stem: The smallest of the eight angles has measure $x°$. What is the value of $x$?
items.explanation: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, the eight angles take only two measures, $x$ and $180 - x$. Exactly three of the four chosen angles are congruent, so the four angles are three copies of one measure and one copy of the other. Call the repeated measure $a$ and the single one $b$, where $a + b = 180$. Then $3a + b = 440$. Subtract the first equation from the second to get $2a = 260$, so $a = 130$ and $b = 50$. Check that you have them the right way round: three $50°$ angles and one $130°$ angle would sum to only $280°$. So the repeated angle is the obtuse one, and the smallest of the eight angles measures $50°$. That gives $x = 50$.

B.why: You took all four angles to be congruent, so you divided $440$ by $4$ to get $110$ and then subtracted from $180$. That ignores the condition that exactly three of the angles are congruent, and four $110°$ angles don't meet it.

C.why: You divided $440$ by $4$ and stopped. Four equal angles break the 'exactly three' condition, and $110$ is the obtuse measure in any case, so it can't be the smallest angle.

D.why: You set up $3a + (180 - a) = 440$ correctly and got $130$, but that is the repeated obtuse angle. The question asks for the smallest angle, which is the one supplementary to it: $180 - 130 = 50$.
